assignments.raw_value: the examination, evaluation, diagnosis, treatment, or performance of preventive procedures related to diseases, disorders, or conditions of the human eyes or adjacent and associated structures, consistent with this chapter and regulations adopted by the board

The practice of optometry is a learned profession involving the examination, measurement by objective and subjective means, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of any departure from the normal of the human eyes, their adjacent structures, and visual system.

The 'practice of optometry' means the examination, diagnosis, treatment, and management of conditions of the human eye, lid, adnexa, and visual system, including the removal of foreign bodies from the cornea, conjunctiva, lid, or adnexa but shall exclude other surgery of the lid, adnexa, or visual system which requires anything other than a topical anesthetic.

The examination or refraction of the human eye and its appendages and the employment of any objective or subjective means or methods other than surgery for the purpose of diagnosing or treating any visual, muscular, neurological or anatomical anomalies of the eye.

Optometrists approved by the board may prescribe and administer pharmaceutical agents for the treatment of the human eye and its adjacent structures, including steroids and narcotic analgesics except Schedule I and II narcotics and Schedule III agents containing Hydrocodone; Schedule III agents limited to 96-hour prescriptions; authority to administer epinephrine/benadryl for anaphylaxis.

Licensed optometrists who meet board qualifications may possess, administer, and prescribe all oral and topical pharmaceutical agents for diagnosis or treatment of conditions of the eye, lids, and adnexa, excluding Schedules I and II controlled substances (except hydrocodone combination drugs in combination with oral analgesic drugs, limited to 72-hour prescriptions with no refills).

A licensee may prescribe, dispense and administer over-the-counter pharmaceuticals, topical prescription pharmaceuticals, specified oral prescription pharmaceuticals for treating diseases of the eye and its adnexa, and schedule III controlled substances that are analgesics. A licensee may use epinephrine delivery systems to counteract an anaphylactic reaction. A licensee may not prescribe schedule I, II, IV or V controlled substances except as specified.

A licensed optometrist who is a therapeutic optometrist may prescribe or use prescription or nonprescription drugs including schedule II controlled narcotic substances limited to hydrocodone combination drugs and schedule III, IV, and V controlled narcotic substances for ocular disease. Schedule I or II narcotics (except hydrocodone combination drugs) are excluded. Injectable drugs are excluded except epinephrine auto-injector for anaphylaxis.

Optometrists may use ocular agents-D (topical diagnostic agents) and ocular agents-T (topical and oral therapeutic agents, excluding controlled substances and injectables). Optometrists authorized to practice advanced optometric care may administer or prescribe pharmaceutical agents including controlled substances under schedules II, III, IV and V for diagnosis and treatment of conditions and diseases of the eye and ocular adnexae, subject to limitations on quantities dispensed; may use injectable medications only to counteract anaphylaxis or anaphylactic reaction; may not prescribe nonemergen

May use epinephrine auto-injector for anaphylaxis. Excludes oral immuno-suppressives (except oral steroids as specified), oral antifungals, oral antimetabolites, substances delivered intravenously or by injection, and medications solely for systemic conditions outside optometric scope.

Certified optometrists may administer and prescribe topical and oral ocular pharmaceutical agents as provided in s. 463.0055. Non-certified licensed practitioners may use topically applied anesthetics solely for glaucoma examinations. Certified optometrists may not administer or prescribe controlled substances listed in Schedule III, IV, or V except for oral analgesics on the formulary for ocular pain relief. Therapeutic pharmaceutical agents shall not include controlled substances enumerated in sections 329-14, 329-16, 329-18, 329-20, and 329-22.

Optometrists may prescribe, administer and dispense therapeutic pharmaceutical agents for treatment of conditions of the eye and/or eyelid upon issuance of a certificate by the state board of optometry, subject to board-approved rules. Certified optometrists may direct licensed nurses and other healthcare personnel to execute diagnostic and therapeutic orders and administer pharmaceutical agents.

Therapeutic advanced glaucoma licensees may prescribe schedules III, IV, and V controlled substances for ocular conditions including glaucoma treatment; schedules I and II are prohibited. Injections are prohibited except for emergency treatment of anaphylactic shock.

Controlled substances in schedules 3, 4, and 5 (including dihydrocodeinone combination drugs) are included; schedule 2 controlled substances, oral cortical steroids are excluded.

Licensed optometrists with the required certificate may prescribe or administer legend drugs for eye and adnexa conditions, subject to limitations: no intravenous, intraocular, sub-Tenon, posterior orbital septum, or intramuscular injections (except Botulinum toxin and anaphylaxis treatment); no Schedule II and III oral legend drugs; no oral steroids for more than 14 days without physician consultation.

Optometrists certified by the board may prescribe and administer pharmaceutical agents (excluding injectable agents), including diagnostic and therapeutic pharmaceutical agents, for examination, diagnosis, and treatment of conditions or diseases of the eye, adnexa, and vision. Certification is required for both diagnostic and therapeutic pharmaceutical agents. Therapeutic pharmaceutical agents must be dispensed by a licensed pharmacist.

Optometrists certified under Sections 73-19-153 through 73-19-165 may prescribe and use therapeutic pharmaceutical agents including over-the-counter medications, prescription medications rational to eye/eyelid conditions (excluding intraocular injection/implantation, dermal fillers, cosmetic injectables, and Schedule I drugs), and epinephrine auto-injection for anaphylaxis. Optometrists certified under Sections 73-19-103 through 73-19-109 may use diagnostic pharmaceutical agents (anesthetics, mydriatics, cycloplegics, dyes, OTC drugs) topically. May administer, dispense, and prescribe: topical diagnostic agents (cycloplegics, mydriatics, topical anesthetics, fluorescein, emergency miotics); oral analgesics codeine, propoxyphene, hydrocodone, and dihydrocodeine alone or in combination with nonscheduled/nonregulated drugs; and board-approved drugs for ocular treatment limited to the anterior segment and adnexa. Glaucoma may be treated.

Optometrists certified by the Board may prescribe and use pharmaceutical agents in the practice of optometry. Dispensing optometrists may dispense legend or prescription drugs (but not controlled substances) to their own patients after registering with the NC Board of Pharmacy.

Optometrists may prescribe diagnostic and therapeutic pharmaceutical agents including topical agents, locally administered agents for primary eye care procedures, oral anti-infectives, oral antihistamines, and oral analgesics for ocular-related disorders. Nonscheduled pharmaceutical agents (except acetaminophen with 30mg codeine) with documented use in ocular treatment are included. Optometrists may not dispense therapeutic pharmaceutical agents except as drug samples at no cost or contact lenses/ophthalmic devices classified as drugs by FDA.

Licensed optometrists may use topical ocular pharmaceutical agents for diagnostic purposes (if certified under 38-2613) and for therapeutic purposes including glaucoma treatment (if certified under 38-2614). Optometrists may also dispense contact lenses containing ocular pharmaceutical agents they are authorized to prescribe.

Licensed optometrists authorized under RSA 327:6-a may prescribe, administer, and dispense a broad formulary of pharmaceutical agents including topical and oral agents, anti-glaucoma agents (with glaucoma certification), vaccines (influenza, COVID-19, shingles), and epinephrine for anaphylaxis. Schedule I and II controlled substances are prohibited. Oral analgesics including class III and IV controlled substances may be prescribed with board approval.

Optometrists may use and prescribe pharmaceutical agents for treating deficiencies, deformities, diseases, or abnormalities of the human eye and adnexae, excluding injections (except for anaphylaxis), and excluding Schedule I and II controlled dangerous substances except as authorized; certified optometrists may prescribe Schedule III, IV, and V controlled dangerous substances and pharmaceutical agents containing hydrocodone regardless of schedule

Optometrists qualified and certified by the board may prescribe or administer all pharmaceutical agents for the diagnosis and treatment of disease of the eye or adnexa; may prescribe hydrocodone and hydrocodone combination medications; may administer epinephrine auto-injections to counter anaphylaxis; shall not prescribe any other controlled substance classified in Schedule I or II.

Licensed optometrists may administer topical diagnostic ophthalmic agents. Optometrists with a pharmaceutical agent certificate may prescribe and administer pharmaceutical agents including analgesic drugs subject to schedule III, IV, or V, but not schedule I or II drugs. Controlled substances may be prescribed only after an optometric examination, in amounts not exceeding 90 MME/day and not lasting more than 72 hours, and may not be refilled without a subsequent examination.

Optometrists may prescribe and use drugs only in accordance with the provisions of Article 143 and commissioner's regulations. Certified optometrists may use diagnostic pharmaceuticals, topical therapeutic pharmaceutical agents, therapeutic pharmaceutical agents for glaucoma/ocular hypertension, and (with additional certification) oral therapeutic pharmaceutical agents.

Licensed optometrists may employ, apply, administer, and prescribe topical ocular pharmaceutical agents and therapeutic pharmaceutical agents including oral anti-infectives, anti-allergy agents, antiglaucoma agents, analgesics (including certain analgesic controlled substances per board rules), anti-inflammatories (with restrictions), and epinephrine by injection for anaphylaxis. May personally furnish therapeutic pharmaceutical agents at no charge in amounts not exceeding a 72-hour supply.

Optometrists may prescribe dangerous drugs and controlled dangerous substances for all schedules except Schedules I and II, but may prescribe hydrocodone or hydrocodone-containing drugs regardless of schedule for up to 5 days. Certification by the Board is required prior to administering or prescribing drugs.

Optometrists may prescribe pharmaceutical agents approved for topical use and nontopical pharmaceutical agents on the optometric nontopical formulary; may prescribe Schedule II hydrocodone-combination drugs; may not prescribe Schedule I and II drugs generally or pharmaceutical agents not on the nontopical formulary.

Optometrists may administer and prescribe all legend and nonlegend drugs by topical or oral routes approved by the board, including codeine and hydrocodone combinations (Schedule II supply limited to 72 hours), for treatment of the eye, eyelids, lacrimal system and conjunctiva, and for glaucoma. Schedule I and Schedule II controlled substances are excluded except for codeine and hydrocodone combinations. Injections are prohibited except epinephrine auto-injectors for anaphylaxis. Therapeutically certified optometrists must be board-certified to prescribe and administer pharmaceutical agents fo

Amplified optometrists may use and prescribe pharmaceutical agents (excluding Schedule I and II, except hydrocodone-containing medications) in the treatment of conditions of the human eye and its appendages, including anterior uveitis and glaucoma, without surgery or other invasive techniques. Schedule III drugs and hydrocodone-containing medications may be prescribed for no more than 72 hours. No optometrist shall deliver any medication by injection.

A therapeutic certified optometrist may purchase, possess, administer, supply, and prescribe pharmaceutical agents including oral and topically applied medications other than Schedule I and II controlled substances (with limited exceptions for reclassified substances). Oral agents are limited to antihistamines, antimicrobial, antiglaucoma, over-the-counter drugs, and analgesics for ocular/ocular adnexal disease. Analgesic prescriptions limited to 7-day supply. No medications may be given by injection or intravenously.

Optometrists may prescribe or administer any pharmaceutical agent rational to the diagnosis and treatment of the human eye and its appendages, except by injection unless otherwise permitted by this chapter. Expanded scope includes intradermal injection of a paralytic agent and intralesional injection of a steroid to treat a chalazion, subject to prerequisites.

Certified optometrists may administer and prescribe pharmaceutical agents for treatment of conditions and diseases of the eye and eyelid; diagnostic pharmaceutical agents (miotics, mydriatics, cycloplegics and anesthetics) applied topically only for diagnostically certified optometrists; may administer benadryl, epinephrine or equivalent medication to counteract anaphylaxis; may use local anesthetic in conjunction with primary care treatment of an eyelid lesion (with certification); prohibited from nondiagnostic ophthalmic lasers, cataract surgery, procedures requiring other than topical anest

Schedule II controlled substances are prohibited except for hydrocodone combination drugs if so scheduled and prescribed in accordance

TPA-certified optometrists may prescribe and administer Schedule II controlled substances consisting of hydrocodone in combination with acetaminophen and Schedules III through VI controlled substances and devices to treat diseases and abnormal conditions of the human eye and its adnexa. Diagnostic pharmaceutical agents (Schedule VI) may be administered topically by all licensed optometrists. Intramuscular epinephrine may be administered for emergency anaphylactic shock.

Licensees may prescribe appropriate pharmaceutical agents for the diagnosis, management, and treatment of the eye and adnexa, including oral therapeutic pharmaceutical agents, subject to consultation requirements for systemic adverse reactions and glaucoma management.

Optometrists certified under RCW 18.53.010(4) may use topical and oral drugs for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes; oral Schedule III–V controlled substances and oral legend drugs are authorized with board/pharmacy commission approval; Schedule II hydrocodone combination products are authorized; Schedule I and II controlled substances (except hydrocodone combination products) are prohibited. Controlled substances may not be prescribed for more than seven days for a single trauma/episode/condition.

Optometrists may use topical ocular diagnostic pharmaceutical agents (with certification/plan under s. 449.17) and therapeutic pharmaceutical agents (with certification under s. 449.18). The secretary, after consultation with the examining board, medical examining board, and pharmacy examining board, promulgates rules specifying which agents may be used. Optometrists may not dispense (other than by prescribing or administering), except for complimentary samples and contact lenses delivering a therapeutic agent.

A certificate holder may administer or prescribe topical pharmaceutical agents for the anterior segment; prescribe oral drugs from the board-established formulary (Schedules III, IV, V, plus oral antibiotics, NSAIDs, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors); prescribe pharmaceutical-delivering contact lenses; administer epinephrine by injection for anaphylaxis; and (with injectable certification) administer additional injectable pharmaceutical agents. Schedule II controlled substances are prohibited except hydrocodone/hydrocodone-containing drugs may be prescribed for no more than three days by an o

An optometrist shall be allowed to administer and prescribe pharmaceutical agents related to the practice of optometry for the treatment of ocular disease, excluding schedule I and II narcotics, but allowing for the prescribing of hydrocodone or hydrocodone containing pharmaceutical agents regardless of schedule.

fields.rationale: States cluster by how they define surgery: some give broad catch-all tissue-alteration language, some enumerate specific prohibited procedure types, some center the definition on laser use, some simply exclude surgery from scope without defining it, and some define surgery broadly but carve out permitted minor/surgical exceptions.

Invasive surgery including injections into the eyeball, cataract surgery, muscle surgery, retinal surgery, radial keratotomy, laser surgery, and cryosurgery.

Surgery of the lid, adnexa, or visual system which requires anything other than a topical anesthetic is excluded from optometric practice; cataract surgery and radial keratotomy surgery are also explicitly prohibited.

An invasive procedure in which in vivo human tissue is cut, burned, vaporized, removed, coagulated or photodisrupted by use of an electrical cautery, a scalpel, a cryoprobe, a laser or ionizing radiation. Surgery does not include nonsurgical procedures, including the removal of superficial foreign bodies or eyelashes or the use of lasers for diagnostic purposes.

Any act in which human tissue is cut, altered, or otherwise infiltrated by any means. It does not mean an act that solely involves the administration or prescribing of a topical or oral therapeutic pharmaceutical.
any procedure in which human tissue is cut, altered, or otherwise infiltrated by mechanical or laser means

The 'practice of advanced optometric care' does not include surgical treatment of glaucoma, treatment of ocular cancer, treatment of infectious diseases of the retina, use of therapeutic lasers, surgical procedures other than noninvasive procedures, use of general anesthesia, procedures that require the cutting or opening of the globe, enucleation of the eye, extraocular muscle surgery or any invasive procedure performed on the human body other than noninvasive procedures performed on the eye or ocular adnexae.

Surgery is prohibited; also prohibited is the use of ophthalmic lasers or other modalities in which tissue is burned, vaporized, cut, or otherwise irreversibly altered by thermal, light-based, electromagnetic, radiation, chemical, ultrasound, infusion, cryotherapy, or similar means.

a procedure using an instrument, including a laser, scalpel, or needle, in which human tissue is cut, burned, scraped except as provided in s. 463.014(4), or vaporized, by incision, injection, ultrasound, laser, infusion, cryotherapy, or radiation. The term includes a procedure using an instrument which requires the closure of human tissue by suture, clamp, or other such device.
Surgery includes refractive or therapeutic laser surgery; invasive surgery is also prohibited for therapeutically certified optometrists.

Surgical procedures requiring injectable or general anesthesia, moderate sedation, penetration of the globe, or use of ophthalmic lasers for ophthalmic surgery within or upon the globe; also specifically: removal of pterygia and Salzmann's nodules, incisional corneal refractive surgery, and strabismus surgery.
Surgery includes the use of lasers for surgical purposes; the statute prohibits optometrists from performing surgery but enumerates specific exceptions.

Surgical procedures are included in optometric practice except those specifically excluded, including: retina laser procedures, LASIK, PRK, nonlaser surgery for eye removal, full-thickness corneal/scleral incision, penetrating keratoplasty, iris/ciliary body incision, vitreous incision, retina incision, crystalline lens extraction, intraocular implants, extraocular muscle surgery, eyelid malignancy or cosmetic/mechanical repair surgery, bony orbit surgery, lacrimal system incisional surgery (other than probing), full-thickness conjunctivoplasty with graft or flap, any nonlaser procedure not co

A procedure upon the human eye in which in vivo human tissue is injected, cut, burned, frozen, sutured, vaporized, coagulated, or photodisrupted by the use of surgical instrumentation such as, but not limited to, a scalpel, cryoprobe, laser, electric cautery, or ionizing radiation.
Invasive surgical procedures are excluded from optometric scope; the statute does not further define 'invasive surgical procedures' but prohibits them under both Section 66B and 66C.

a procedure using any instruments, including lasers, scalpels, needles, cautery, a cryoprobe, or sutures in which human tissue is cut, burned, vaporized, removed, or otherwise permanently altered by any mechanical means, laser, ionizing radiation, ultrasound, or other means
Invasive surgery is prohibited; tissue-altering lasers are also prohibited

'Invasive procedures' means: (i) The use of lasers other than for observation. (ii) The use of ionizing radiation. (iii) The use of therapeutic ultrasound. (iv) The administration of medication by injection. (v) Procedures that include an incision.
invasive surgery including, but not limited to, surgery using lasers
Surgery includes the use of lasers for treatment of any disease or condition or for the correction of refractive error.

Intraocular surgical procedures are prohibited except those specifically allowed in the statute; the statute also excludes intraocular injection, intraocular implantation, biopsy of any part of the globe, intraocular aspiration or penetration, and reconstructive surgical procedures on the eyelid.
Surgery is excluded from the definition of optometry practice; the statute defines optometry as examination and treatment 'other than surgery'

Any procedure in which human tissue is cut, altered, or otherwise infiltrated by mechanical means, including use of lasers for therapeutic and photorefractive purposes, ionizing radiation, therapeutic ultrasound, or medication administered by injection; removal of superficial foreign bodies from the eye, adnexa or eyelid is not considered surgery.

Surgery is excluded from the practice of optometry except for enumerated in-office minor surgical procedures: non-laser removal/destruction/drainage of superficial eyelid lesions and conjunctival cysts; removal of nonperforating foreign bodies from cornea, conjunctiva and eyelid; non-laser corneal debridement, culture, scrape or anterior puncture (not including removal of pterygium, corneal biopsy or removal of corneal neoplasias); removal of eyelashes; probing, dilation, irrigation or closure of tear drainage structures; scalpel use only on skin surrounding the eye.

Any procedure using a laser, scalpel, needle or other instrument in which any human tissue is cut, burned or vaporized by incision, injection, ultrasound, laser, infusion, cryotherapy, radiation or other means; or any procedure using an instrument which requires the closure of human tissue by suture, clamp or similar device.

Invasive modality means any procedure in which human tissue is cut, altered, or otherwise infiltrated by mechanical or other means. Invasive modality includes surgery, lasers, ionizing radiation, therapeutic ultrasound and the removal of foreign bodies from within the tissue of the eye.

Any procedure that involves cutting or otherwise infiltrating human tissue by mechanical means including surgery, laser surgery, ionizing radiation, therapeutic ultrasound, administering medication by injection, or the removal of intraocular foreign bodies.
Laser surgery procedures (excluding retina, LASIK, and cosmetic lid surgery) and nonlaser surgery procedures as authorized by the Board are within the practice of optometry.
invasive or laser surgery

Surgery, including, but not limited to, diagnostic, exploratory, palliative, therapeutic, rehabilitative, cosmetic, reconstructive, refractive, light-based or laser surgery; or the use of lasers for therapeutic purposes.
Surgery is not defined in the statute, but optometrists are prohibited from performing surgery and may only treat conditions 'without surgery or other invasive techniques'.

Surgery includes, but is not limited to, an invasive procedure using instruments that require closure by suturing, clamping, or other similar devices or a procedure in which the presence or assistance of a nurse anesthetist or an anesthesiologist is required.
The term 'any means or method' does not include surgeries, unless otherwise permitted by this chapter

Surgical procedures requiring other than a topical anesthetic are prohibited; reconstructive surgical procedures on the eyelid are prohibited; radial keratotomy is prohibited; nondiagnostic ophthalmic lasers are prohibited.

A procedure using instruments, including lasers, scalpels, or needles, in which human tissue is cut, burned, vaporized, or otherwise altered by any mechanical means, laser, or ionizing radiation. Includes procedures using instruments that require closing by suturing, clamping, or another device. Does not include a noninvasive procedure to remove a superficial foreign body in the conjunctiva, eyelid, or corneal epithelium that has not perforated the Bowman's membrane.
Surgery in which human tissue is cut, burned, or vaporized by means of laser or ionizing radiation (for laser surgery); general surgery prohibition applies to all surgery

Treatment through revision, destruction, incision or other structural alteration of human tissue using laser technology; or structural alteration of the human body by the incision or cutting into of tissue for the purpose of diagnostic or therapeutic treatment of conditions or disease processes by any instrument causing localized alteration or transposition of live human tissue.

Any invasive procedure in which human tissue is cut, ablated, or otherwise penetrated by incision, injection, laser, ultrasound, or other means, in order to: Treat human eye diseases; alter or correct refractive error; or alter or enhance cosmetic appearance.
Surgery is excluded from optometric practice except as provided in the defined scope (par. (a)); no further statutory definition of 'surgery' is provided.
